text:
17/ But, in the end, the risky path is not privacy. It is radical transparency.

Transparency makes Ethereum governable, pressureable, and punishable.

Privacy narrows the attack surface. For users, developers, and validators.

Privacy is not the problem. Privacy is existential.
author: ethereum

text:
16/ That is the idea behind Coin Center’s John Hancock Project:

We can and should leverage privacy-preserving credentials and proofs that can satisfy legitimate policy goals without exposing everyone’s identity. 

https://t.co/0NG1OmbxqD
author: ethereum

text: 15/ This does not mean ignoring crime, fraud, or national security. It means giving governments better tools than mass surveillance.
author: ethereum

text:
14/ Intermediary minimization is part of the same project.

If users rely on intermediaries to transact, preserve privacy, query the chain, or avoid censorship, those intermediaries become weak links in a privacy chain.
author: ethereum

text:
13/ I am happy to see CROPS becoming a priority.

Don’t make privacy optional. Make it an Ethereum core guarantee.

Make privacy first-class. Design wallets, L2s, DeFi, identity, social, mempools, and interfaces to leak less by default.
author: ethereum

text:
12/ Ethereum today cannot be credibly neutral because it is too transparent.

Privacy islands on Ethereum may be neutral but they will not survive as islands.

Vires in numeris. Strength (as in privacy and neutrality) only in numbers.
author: ethereum

text:
11/ Two rules follow:

1. Nothing transparent remains neutral.
2. Nothing neutral survives unless it is big enough.

A visible ledger eventually becomes a mediated ledger.
author: ethereum

text:
10/ “If you truly want neutral infrastructure. If you truly want dumb pipes. The pipes need to be actually blind to the shit that flows through them.” 

https://t.co/hAmv6J5Dkk
author: ethereum

text:
9/ Willful blindness is not a defense.

But actual blindness is different, and may actually protect neutral infrastructure.
author: ethereum

text: 8/ If you regularly profit from your ability to see transactions onchain, e.g. MEV, it’s going to be hard to argue you couldn’t also help law enforcement profit from that knowledge.
author: ethereum

text:
7/ There’s a deeper warning here on validator liability:

If you can see alleged fraud, sanctions exposure, or money laundering, someone may argue you helped facilitate it.
author: ethereum

text:
6/ Coin Center challenged the Tornado Cash sanctions because immutable smart contracts are not people or property, and sanctioning software crossed a legal line.

But Ethereum could make those fights less necessary by making private infrastructure the default.
author: ethereum
quoted_text:
0/ The Tornado Cash legal saga continues.

Alex Pertsev is still fighting for his freedom.

Guest thread by @ameensol spotlighting @alex_pertsev's legal case in the Netherlands and the ongoing battle to protect privacy. 🧵 https://t.co/HzYq0odpzh

text:
5/ Tornado Cash, the once sanctioned smart contract, is often treated as proof that privacy is dangerous.

It really shows us that privacy tools that exist as small islands on transparent chains are easy to isolate, demonize, sanction, and prosecute.
author: ethereum

text:
4/ If infrastructure can see everything, it will be pressured to act on what it sees. That turns neutral infrastructure into mediated infrastructure.

Neutrality requires blindness: the more a pipe can see, the less it can remain a dumb pipe. 

https://t.co/pOZ1ScDiv0
author: ethereum

text:
3/ A fully transparent ledger gives governments, prosecutors, corporations, analytics firms, intermediaries, and validators too much knowledge.

Knowing becomes pressure: stop this transaction, block that user, explain what you knew, exploit that opportunity.
author: ethereum

text:
2/ Many believe that onchain privacy means regulators will assume criminality and non-compliance. This has become almost instinctive in crypto policy circles. Over time, I think this will invert.

Privacy is not a vulnerability. I worry more about transparency.
author: ethereum
